Chapter 9—Sustaining Change: Building a Culture of Clarity and Trust.
You know, real change doesn't just happen overnight. If you want to truly transform a team or an entire organization, those core practices—like setting clear goals, offering quick praise, and making timely corrections—they can't just be one-off initiatives. They need to become the heartbeat of your culture, part of the shared way everyone thinks and works.
This takes commitment. Not just from one or two leaders—but from folks at every level, backed by the broader organization. So, how do you actually build that kind of culture?
One powerful way is through storytelling. When people share real examples—maybe about how a clear goal helped a team member succeed, or how immediate praise boosted someone’s confidence—it makes those practices come alive. Leaders can highlight these moments in team meetings, send out stories in newsletters, or just talk about them in everyday conversations. It helps everyone see these principles in action, not just as ideas on a poster.
Another big piece is alignment. Imagine if the same values—clarity, recognition, accountability—show up everywhere, from hiring and onboarding to performance reviews. When people see that these aren’t just buzzwords, but a real way of life, it sets a standard. New team members pick up on it fast, and everyone feels encouraged to live up to those expectations.
Want to reinforce that culture even more? Here are a few ways that really work:
Celebrate milestones and progress—not just the final results. Recognize the small wins along the way.
Encourage peer-to-peer recognition. That way, praise comes from all directions, not just from the top.
And make sure everyone has the training and resources they need to give and receive feedback. It helps people grow and keeps communication open.
Over time, these efforts create a positive feedback loop. As people see the benefits—like greater trust, stronger results, and a more supportive environment—they become more invested in keeping it going. The culture starts to reinforce itself, which makes it so much easier to handle challenges and adapt to changes.
Here’s a great real-world example. In one healthcare organization, leaders started holding regular “huddle” meetings. Teams would review their goals, share successes, and talk about challenges in these quick, focused check-ins. Over time, these huddles became a cornerstone of their culture, helping everyone stay connected and motivated—even during stressful times.
When leaders put culture first, those core practices—clarity, recognition, and accountability—really start to stick. Even if people come and go, or circumstances change, the organization remains strong. In the end, you get a workplace where those values are woven into every interaction, every single day.
